Consult Summary:
- 45-year-old female housekeeper with 3–4 months of progressively painful, itchy, cracked palmar skin affecting work.
- Clinician impression: dermatitis, likely contact/irritant dermatitis related to occupational exposure; prescription topical steroid and emollient therapy provided with advice to avoid triggers and early follow-up.

Problem List:

Issue 1: Palmar dermatitis / suspected contact dermatitis
- Presenting problem: painful, itchy, cracked skin on the palms for approximately 3–4 months; occasionally bleeds after scratching.
- Progression/impact: symptoms have worsened to the point of impairing ability to work; off work for past 3 days.
- Exposures/social factors: works as a hotel housekeeper using bathroom cleaning products; recently changed jobs 4 months ago; not consistently wearing gloves.
- Prior treatments tried: E45 emollient — no significant benefit; antihistamine — ineffective (name/dose not documented).
- Clinical impression: clinician suspects dermatitis, likely contact/irritant dermatitis related to cleaning products.
- Management provided: prescription for topical steroid cream (name/dose/route/frequency not documented) and recommendation for stronger emollients to be applied 3–4 times daily for the next couple of weeks; strict avoidance of triggers and consistent use of gloves while cleaning advised.
- Follow-up: return in 1–2 weeks if not improved (10–14 days suggested) or sooner if symptoms worsen or spread.
- Specialist/allied review: none documented.
- Differential: dermatitis / contact dermatitis (as stated by clinician).

Issue 2: Type 2 diabetes mellitus
- History: patient reports diagnosis of type 2 diabetes.
- Medications: taking metformin (dose/route/frequency not documented).
- Review of systems: patient reports feeling generally well; no fever, nausea/vomiting, bowel or urinary problems reported.
- Examination/findings: none documented in transcript specific to diabetes.
- Management: diabetes care ongoing; no changes or diabetes-specific advice documented in this consult.

Issue 3: Generalized dry skin (xerosis)
- Description/timeline: patient reports mild longstanding dryness on legs and other areas; less severe than hand symptoms.
- Impact: not severe; no specific treatment documented apart from general emollient advice for hand management.
- Management: stronger emollients recommended for hands; no specific plan documented for generalized dryness.

Medications:
- Metformin — dose/route/frequency not documented.
- E45 emollient — tried over the counter, no benefit (dose/route/frequency not documented).
- Antihistamine — name/dose/route/frequency not documented (tried, no benefit).
- Topical steroid cream — prescribed, name/dose/route/frequency not documented.
- Stronger emollient(s) — recommended, name/dose/route/frequency not documented.

Allergies:
- No known drug or other allergies reported.

Past Medical History:
- Type 2 diabetes mellitus.
- No known prior skin diagnoses (patient reports no eczema/dermatitis diagnosis).

Social History:
- Occupation: hotel housekeeper (commercial cleaning of bedrooms, bathrooms, corridors).
- Workplace exposure: frequent use of bathroom cleaning products; inconsistent glove use.
- Work impact: unable to work for 3 days due to hand symptoms.
- Smoking: denies smoking.
- Alcohol: reports a couple of pints per week.
- Living arrangements: not documented.

Preventative History:
- No preventative care (cervical screening, mammogram, PSA, FOBT, BMD, vaccinations, optometry, skin check) documented in transcript.

Physical Examination:
- Vitals: none documented.
- Skin/exam findings: no formal physical examination findings recorded in transcript (patient described cracked, itchy, painful palmar skin; clinician did not document objective exam details).

Plan:
- Immediate: prescription for topical steroid cream sent to patient’s pharmacy (specific agent/dose not documented).
- Topical emollient therapy: start stronger emollients and apply 3–4 times daily to affected areas for the next couple of weeks.
- Trigger avoidance: advise consistent use of protective gloves when cleaning and avoidance of offending cleaning products where possible.
- Return precautions: revisit in 1–2 weeks (10–14 days) if no improvement, or sooner if symptoms worsen, spread, or significantly impair function.
- Further steps if no improvement: clinician stated alternative treatments could be considered at follow-up (not specified).

- Internal conflicts: none identified in the transcript.
